content_html:
A new study from Caltech uses a mathematical framework borrowed from cosmology to analyze ocean data and characterize individual flow features in the churning chaos. With the technique, the researchers are able to measure and characterize features in maps of the ocean surface, allowing them to differentiate ocean flows that otherwise look identical when evaluated with standard analysis tools.

The work is important for sharpening our understanding of ocean physics and for improving ocean and climate models, which must capture not just how energetic the ocean's motions are but also their structure.

The research was led by Jack Skinner, a former postdoctoral scholar in the Caltech lab of Jörn Callies, professor of oceanography and environmental science, in collaboration with physicist Albion Lawrence of Brandeis University. A paper describing the work appears in the journal Science Advances.

From currents to filaments

The ocean is incredibly complex. Take the Gulf Stream, for example. This major current, roughly 60 miles (97 kilometers) wide and originating between the Florida Keys and Cuba, carries heat up the eastern coast of North America and across toward Europe.

As the current flows, it can fold and fragment into large-scale vortices—essentially enormous whirlpools—that can then elongate into long filaments or break up into even smaller vortices. Such processes occur constantly in oceans all across the planet, and understanding them and other ocean features is important for accurately modeling the ocean and predicting how it impacts our climate.

Measuring structure beyond energy

Typical measurements of ocean features (and fluid dynamics in general) use a tool called the power spectrum, a measure of the energy present at various scales, from planetary-scale currents to ocean eddies to tiny wavelets. However, a power spectrum does not give information about the structure of these features. It cannot, for instance, distinguish between round but isolated ocean vortices and deformed vortices trailing thin filaments into nearby waters.

For the present work, the researchers turned to a mathematical tool called the scattering transform, which has been previously used in cosmology to study the distribution of matter across the universe.

"The scattering transform provides a way to quantitatively measure shape and structure, like how sparse or clustered certain features are in a given image," says Skinner, who is now at UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography. By using the scattering transform, the researchers were able to tell apart waves, eddies and different types of turbulence even when their power spectra are identical.

"It also tells you about the anisotropy, a measurement of whether the shapes are circular, blobby or elongated," Skinner adds. "This helps us understand the different structures in the ocean and how they are dynamically mixing and evolving in time."

Reading SWOT's ocean maps

The team found that the scattering transform technique is especially well suited to extracting information from data such as the data obtained by the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) space mission, launched in 2022, which is mapping the topography of Earth's surface water—including oceans, major lakes, rivers and wetlands. SWOT measures bumps and dips in water levels at unprecedented resolution.

The satellite creates a global map every 21 days, but because it only revisits each given location every three weeks, structures like waves cannot be distinguished from eddies based on how quickly they change in time. These features could be distinguished using the scattering transform, the researchers say.

"For decades, we've analyzed the height of the ocean surface from altimetry along one-dimensional satellite tracks, and the power spectrum has been a natural tool for that," Skinner says. "SWOT gives us an unprecedented two-dimensional and high-resolution view of the ocean from space, which means we can develop new tools that study the structure of ocean flows."

The researchers are next applying the technique to SWOT data and extending it to other challenges in Earth science such as identifying transitions in types of sea ice as it freezes and melts over the seasonal cycle.

Publication details
